about: Sections of the AI from scratch lessons (ihor.sh/ai), split into overlapping ~100-word pieces, with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings of 'lesson: section. piece' (384 numbers, unit length × 127, int8, base64, one row per piece).

sections.section: 1. Rules you write vs rules you learn
sections.text: A normal program follows rules a person wrote: "sales tax is 8.875% of the price". That works when someone can write the rule. Now try writing the rule for "this photo contains a cat". Pointy ears? Some cats have folded ears. Whiskers? So do dogs. Every rule breaks. Machine learning flips it around. Instead of the rule, you give the computer examples with answers : ten thousand photos, each labeled "cat" or "not cat". The computer finds a rule that matches the examples, and you hope it works on photos it has never seen. That hope, and making sure it's justified, is most of the job. A normal program follows rules a person wrote; a model finds its rule from examples that come with answers.

sections.section: 2. A model is a function with knobs
sections.text: Here's a small, made-up example: 40 taxi rides, each a dot. Across is how far the ride went, up is how many minutes it took. We want to predict the time for a ride we haven't taken yet. The simplest guess is a straight line:  \text{minutes} = a \times \text{km} + b  That formula is the model , and a and b are its knobs (ML people call them parameters or weights ). a is minutes per kilometer; b is the time every ride costs no matter how short: getting in, the first red light. Turn the knobs and try to make the blue line run through the middle of the dots. Each red stick is one ride's mistake: how far the line's guess is from what really happened. a (minutes per km) b (minutes at the start) Let the computer train it How do we say how good a line is, with one number? Square each red stick (so misses above and below both count, and big misses count a lot) and average them. That's the mean squared error , the readout above. Getting it small is the whole goal. A good fit here gets it down to about 8.5; you can't reach zero, because two rides of the same length don't take the same time. Traffic is noise no line can predict. A model is a formula with knobs, and one number, the error, says how good a setting of the knobs is.

sections.section: 3. Training: let the computer turn the knobs
sections.text: Press Let the computer train it . The computer does what you did, but carefully: for each knob it asks "if I nudge you up a tiny bit, does the error go up or down?", then moves every knob a small step in the direction that lowers the error, and repeats. The strip under the picture shows the error after each step. That loop is training , and the method is called gradient descent . Stage 1 shows exactly how the computer gets the "up or down" answer (it's a derivative), and stage 2 shows the same loop training a neural network. One honest warning: the real test of a model is rides it hasn't seen. A model that fits its examples perfectly but fails on new ones is useless, and that trap, called overfitting , gets a whole lesson in stage 3. Training is turning every knob a little in the direction that lowers the error, over and over.

kind what you give it examples Supervised examples with the right answers ride → minutes; photo → "cat"; email → spam or not; sentence → next word (that's how chatbots are trained) Unsupervised examples with no answers; find structure group customers who behave alike; spot an unusual night on the subway Reinforcement a world to act in and a score (reward) a game-playing program; a robot learning to walk; tuning a chatbot from people's thumbs up The taxi model was supervised: every ride came with its true time. Most ML at work is supervised. Supervised learning learns from answers; the other kinds find structure without answers, or learn from rewards.

Training is maybe a tenth of the job. The rest is a loop, and this path teaches every step of it: step the question where you learn it Frame What exactly are we predicting, and how will we know it's good enough? stage 3 Data Where do examples come from? Are the answers right? Is anything leaking the answer? stages 3–4 Baseline What does the simplest possible model score? stage 3 Model Which model, which knobs, and how to train it stages 1, 2, 4, 5 Evaluate How good is it on data it never saw, and where does it fail? stage 3 Ship and watch Make it fast and cheap, put it in front of users, notice when the world changes stages 6–7 Training is a small part of the job; the rest is getting good data, measuring honestly, and keeping the model working.

Boxes marked Your turn ask you to predict before you're told: guessing first, even wrong, is how it sticks. Sliders and dots in pictures can be dragged. And code boxes run right in the page. Try this one: press Run , then change a number and run it again. Don't worry if the code looks foreign: the next lesson teaches exactly enough to read and change everything on this path. And Blip, the companion in the corner, can answer questions about whatever page you're on.

print(...) shows whatever you put between the brackets; separate several things with commas. * is times, / is divide, ** is "to the power of", and text goes in quotes. Lines starting with # are comments: notes for people, ignored by the computer. import math brings in square roots, e^x and logs. Python is a calculator first: numbers, operations and print.

A variable is a name for a value, so you can use it later. = doesn't mean "equals" here, it means "from now on, this name holds this": so x = x + 1 is fine, it means "x becomes one more than it was" (short form: x += 1 ). A variable is a name for a value, and = means "becomes", not "equals".

ML is about many examples at once, so you'll constantly hold lists of numbers. A list is written with square brackets. Items are numbered from 0 : the first item is xs[0] , and xs[-1] is the last. len(xs) is how many there are, and xs.append(v) adds one to the end. A list holds many values in order, numbered from 0.

sections.section: 4. Loops: do it for every item
sections.text: A loop repeats code. for x in xs: runs the indented lines below it once per item. range(1, 6) counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (it stops before the second number). Python uses indentation to say what's inside the loop: four spaces, no curly braces. Adding things up in a loop is the most common pattern on this path: the mean, the error, the gradient. A loop runs the same indented lines once for every item.

A function takes inputs and gives back an output, exactly like a function in math. def starts one, the indented lines are its recipe, and return hands back the answer. A model is a function: input in, prediction out. A function is a named recipe: inputs in, one answer out. A model is a function.

A comparison asks a yes-or-no question and answers True or False : > , < , >= , == (is equal: two signs, because one = means "becomes") and != (is not equal). if runs its indented lines only when the answer is True , and else when it isn't; and and or join two questions. Four more shapes you'll meet in every notebook. A dictionary , {"key": value} , looks values up by name. A named argument , predict(4, b=10) , sets one of a function's settings by name: you'll see figsize=(6, 3) and lr=0.01 everywhere. An f-string , f"... {x} ..." , puts values into text. And lambda x: 2 * x is a one-line function without a name, for when something wants a function as its input: the notebooks' check(lambda: ...) uses one to test your answer when you run it. Comparisons answer True or False, if picks a path, and dictionaries look values up by name.

Real ML code almost never loops over numbers one by one. NumPy arrays hold many numbers and do arithmetic on all of them at once: a * km + b with km an array computes every ride's guess in one step. It's shorter, it reads like the math, and it's a hundred times faster, because the loop runs inside NumPy's compiled code. Everybody imports it as np . A NumPy array does the same arithmetic on every number at once, without a loop.

matplotlib draws charts; everyone imports its plotting part as plt . This box reuses the rides from the box above (it runs that one quietly first) and plots the error for many values of the knob a: A chart is the fastest way to see what a list of numbers is doing.

Real data comes as tables: rows of examples, named columns of features. pandas (imported as pd ) holds a table in a DataFrame , and it can add columns, summarize, filter and group in a line each. The last line of a box, if it's just a value, is shown, so a DataFrame shows as a table. A comparison on a column gives a column of True / False . Because True counts as 1, its .sum() is how many and its .mean() is what share , and putting it in df[...] keeps only those rows. groupby splits the table by a column and summarizes each part. Stage 4 goes deep into pandas and scikit-learn; this is enough until then. A DataFrame is a table with named columns, and most questions about it take one line.

sections.section: 10. Where to run real code: notebooks
sections.text: The boxes on these pages are for small experiments. Real ML work happens in notebooks : documents mixing code, output and notes, run on a machine with a GPU. Two free places run them in your browser, no install: Google Colab and Kaggle . Every lesson on this path has a practice notebook that opens in either with one click; that's where you'll use PyTorch (stage 2 onward), which is too big to run inside a web page. Notebooks mix code, output and notes, and run free in the browser on Colab or Kaggle.

A function takes a number in and gives a number out. f(x) = x^2 says "call the input x, the output is x times x": so f(3) = 9. The graph of a function is every pair (input, output) drawn as a dot: across is the input, up is the output. Pick a function and drag x: the yellow dot is (x, f(x)). function f(x) = 2x + 1 (a line) f(x) = x² (a bowl) f(x) = eˣ (grows fast) f(x) = ln x (grows slowly) f(x) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ˣ) (an S) x You'll meet all five again. The line is the taxi model from Start 1. The bowl is what an error looks like as you turn a knob: one lowest point, and training rolls into it. e^x and \ln x are the next two sections. The S-curve , called the sigmoid , squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1, so a model can turn a score into a probability (chapter 3 builds a neuron with it). Many functions take several inputs : f(a, b) = a \times 4 + b is the taxi model's guess for a 4 km ride as you turn both knobs. Stage 1 draws functions of two inputs as landscapes you walk over. A function turns an input number into an output number, and its graph is every such pair drawn as a dot.

sections.section: 2. Powers, and very big and very small numbers
sections.text: 2^5 means five 2s multiplied: 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 32. Three rules follow just from counting how many copies get multiplied: rule example why a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n} 2^3 \times 2^4 = 2^7 = 128 3 copies, then 4 more a^{-n} = 1 / a^n 2^{-3} = 1/8 = 0.125 each step down the powers divides by 2: 8, 4, 2, 1, ½, ¼, ⅛ a^{1/2} = \sqrt{a} 9^{1/2} = 3 9^{1/2} \times 9^{1/2} = 9^1, so it's the number that squares to 9 ML numbers come in wildly different sizes: a learning rate of 0.001, a model with 7,000,000,000 weights. Scientific notation writes them as a number times a power of 10: 0.001 = 10^{-3} and 7{,}000{,}000{,}000 = 7 \times 10^9. Code writes the same thing as 1e-3 and 7e9 : "e" here means "times ten to the", nothing to do with the number e. The number e \approx 2.718 is special because e^x grows at a rate equal to its own value (Calculus 1 shows why that makes it the easy one). You'll mostly see it in e^x, written np.exp(x) in code. A power counts how many copies are multiplied, and scientific notation tames very big and very small numbers.

A logarithm answers "what power?". \log_2 8 = 3 because 2^3 = 8: it counts how many 2s you multiply to get 8. \log_{10} 1000 = 3 counts the zeros. And the natural log \ln x is the power of e: \ln x = t means e^t = x. So \ln undoes e^x, and the two graphs are mirror images across the dashed line y = x. Drag t: t The one rule that matters most in ML: a log turns multiplying into adding , \ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b. (It follows from the first power rule: multiplying powers of e adds the exponents.) A model's probability of a whole dataset is the product of its probabilities for each example: thousands of numbers below 1 multiplied together. That underflows to exactly 0 on a computer, so models work with the sum of the logs instead. Run it: A logarithm counts multiplications, so it turns multiplying into adding.

sections.section: 4. The Σ sign is a loop
sections.text: The big Greek S, \Sigma (sigma), means "add these up". The bits around it say what to add:  \sum_{i=1}^{4} i^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 = 30  Read it as: "for i from 1 to 4, add up i^2". Underneath is where the counter starts, on top is where it stops, and to the right is what you add each time. It's exactly the loop from Start 2. Change the sum below: add up i i² 1 / 2ⁱ 2 for i from 1 to n = Datasets are written with a counter too: x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n are the n examples, and x_i is "the i-th one". With that, the mean is  \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i  "x-bar is one over n times the sum of all the x's": add them up, divide by how many. (The 1/n out front does the dividing.) And a product of many terms uses the big Greek P, \prod, the same way. Σ is a loop written in math: start, stop, and what to add each time.

ML borrows Greek letters for its knobs and settings. There are only a handful, and each one is used for the same thing almost everywhere: symbol say it usually means w, b w, b weights and bias: a model's knobs \theta theta all the knobs together \eta or \alpha eta, alpha learning rate: how big a step training takes \lambda lambda how hard to punish big weights (regularization, stage 3) \sigma sigma (small) the sigmoid function, or a spread (standard deviation) \mu mu a mean \epsilon epsilon a tiny number, or noise \hat{y} y-hat the model's guess (the true answer is plain y) L L the loss: one number saying how wrong the model is \nabla L grad L, the gradient which way each knob should move to raise the loss (stage 1) \approx, \leftarrow, \in about, becomes, is in x \in [0, 1]: x is between 0 and 1; w \leftarrow w - 1: w becomes w − 1 \mathbf{x}, W bold x, capital W a list of numbers (a vector) and a table of numbers (a matrix), chapter 1 Don't memorize the table: come back to it. After a few lessons the letters read like words. A handful of Greek letters do the same jobs almost everywhere: come back to the table until they read like words.

Every formula is a sentence. Read it left to right, say each symbol's name, and turn it into a recipe. Try each one before revealing. Here are all three formulas as code. Notice how directly each line matches its formula: One small trap: math counts examples from 1 (x_1 to x_n), code counts from 0 ( xs[0] to xs[n - 1] ). Same examples, shifted labels. Every formula is a sentence and a recipe: read it left to right and it turns into code.

Training produces a file of numbers: the weights. To be useful, three more things wrap around it: Input A photo from a person: any size, any format. → Preprocess Resize and scale it into exactly the array shape and range the model was trained on. → Model The architecture plus the saved weights: numbers in, scores out. → Postprocess Scores → probabilities → the top few labels, shown in the interface. Get the preprocessing even slightly different from training (another image size, colors in a different order, a missing normalization) and a model that scored 95% in testing quietly turns useless. It's the most common deployment bug, so sections 3 and 4 do both steps by hand. A deployed model is weights plus the exact preprocessing, the code that turns scores into an answer, and an app around them.

Below is MobileNet, a small network trained on ImageNet (1.2 million photos, 1,000 categories), running entirely in your browser. Pick a photo, or use the sample. Its top five guesses and their probabilities appear next to it. your photo Sample: a dog Sample: a NYC street Loading the model (about 4 MB)… The street sample gets odd answers ("scoreboard", "mobile home"): ImageNet photos show one main object, so a busy street is outside what MobileNet learned. For counting cars, a detector is the right tool (chapter 9). Try something that isn't in its 1,000 categories at all, like a face, a drawing, or a screenshot. It still answers, often confidently. A classifier can only choose among the labels it knows; nothing in it says "none of these". That's worth remembering when you put your own model in front of people. A model trained on certain photos answers best on photos like them, and always answers with one of its classes.

sections.section: 3. What the model needs from a photo
sections.text: Pretrained image models expect the exact recipe used in training. For the ImageNet family it's: resize so the short side is 256 pixels, cut the central 224×224 square, scale pixel values from 0–255 to 0–1, then normalize each color channel with ImageNet's mean and standard deviation, and arrange the array as (batch, channels, height, width). Here's that recipe on a made-up 300×400 image: Resize, crop, scale and normalize exactly as in training, or the model quietly gets worse.

The network returns one score per class, called logits . Softmax (chapter 5) turns them into probabilities; the app shows the top few. Gradio's label widget expects exactly this: a dictionary from label to probability. Softmax turns the network's scores into probabilities, and a careful app shows the top few, not just one.

sections.section: 5. The app: Gradio, and a home on Hugging Face Spaces
sections.text: Gradio is a Python library that builds a web interface around any function: you say what goes in (an image) and what comes out (a label with probabilities), and it makes the page. This is a whole app, the one the practice notebook writes as app.py : Hugging Face Spaces hosts apps like this for free (a small CPU, which is plenty for one image at a time). A Space is a Git repository with three files: app.py , requirements.txt (the libraries), and the model files. Push them and Spaces installs, starts the app and gives it a public address. The notebook does it with the huggingface_hub library in a few lines, using a free account's access token. Gradio builds the page around a function, and a Hugging Face Space hosts it free from three files.

A vector is a pair of numbers, (x, y) , but it's easier to think of it as an arrow from the origin: go x steps right, y steps up. Drag the tip of the blue arrow . In machine learning, everything becomes a vector: a pixel image is a long list of brightness values, a word becomes a list of a few hundred numbers. Same idea, just with more than two directions to walk in. The picture An arrow: how far right, how far up. Its length is how far the tip is from the start. The math A list of numbers v = (v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n). Its length comes from Pythagoras: \lVert v \rVert = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \dots + v_n^2}.

sections.section: 2. Adding is walking one arrow, then the other
sections.text: To add two vectors, walk along the first, then from its tip along the second. Where you end up is the sum. Drag both tips. Notice you can go around the parallelogram either way and land in the same spot: a + b = b + a . The picture Walk a, then walk b. Stretching an arrow by 2 doubles each step. The math Add and scale coordinate by coordinate: a + b = (a_1 + b_1,\ a_2 + b_2), \ c\,a = (c\,a_1,\ c\,a_2). One more operation, the most important one in this whole course: the dot product . Multiply matching coordinates and add them up: a \cdot b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2. It's one number, and it measures how much two arrows point the same way : big and positive when they agree, zero when they're at right angles, negative when they oppose. The readout above shows it live; drag b around a and watch the sign flip as it crosses the right angle.  a \cdot b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 = \lVert a \rVert\,\lVert b \rVert \cos\theta  Remember this one. A neuron (chapter 3) is a dot product of inputs and weights. Attention (chapter 7) is dot products between words. A matrix, next section, is a stack of dot products. The dot product is one number for how much two arrows agree: their lengths multiplied, times the cosine of the angle between them.

sections.section: 3. A matrix moves the whole plane
sections.text: Here's the big idea. Two special arrows, î = (1, 0) and ĵ = (0, 1), are the plane's "steps". Any vector is "x of the first step plus y of the second". Now drag the tips of î and ĵ . The grid follows, and so does every vector on it, because v is still x of the new î plus y of the new ĵ. Rotate 90° Shear Flip Squash flat Reset That's all a 2×2 matrix is: the columns say where î and ĵ land. Multiplying a vector by the matrix means "find where it lands". The shaded square started with area 1; its new area is the determinant . It goes negative when space gets flipped over, and zero when the plane is squashed onto a line. Then information is lost: many vectors land on the same spot, and you can't undo the move. A matrix is a move of the whole plane. Its columns are where the two steps land, and every other arrow follows, because every arrow is made of those steps.

sections.section: 4. A neural network layer: a move, then a bend
sections.text: If you stack matrices you only get another matrix: still straight lines, still a single move. Networks get their power from one tiny extra step after each matrix: a bend . The most common one, ReLU, just says "negative numbers become zero". Watch what it does to the moved grid: everything left of the vertical axis gets folded onto it, everything below the horizontal axis onto that. Apply the bend (ReLU) Reset Drag î and ĵ again: the layer is "move, then fold". Stack dozens of these, each with its own matrix, and the folds can carve space into almost any shape, like one region for "cat" and another for "dog". Training a network is searching for the matrices that put the folds in the right places. That's where we're headed: next chapter, gradients , how a network finds which way to nudge every number. A layer is a move, then a fold. Without the fold, any stack of layers is still a single move. Inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra , which goes much deeper. All lessons: AI from scratch .

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.text: A coffee and two bagels cost $7. Three coffees and a bagel cost $11. What does each cost? Call a coffee x and a bagel y:  \begin{aligned} x + 2y &= 7 \\ 3x + y &= 11 \end{aligned}  Each equation on its own allows many answers: every point on a line. The blue line is every (x, y) with x + 2y = 7, the yellow line every one with 3x + y = 11. The answer has to be on both, so it's where they cross . Drag the dots to tilt and move each line. Coffee and bagels Parallel Same line twice Two lines can do only three things: cross once ( one answer ), run side by side ( no answer ), or lie on top of each other ( infinitely many ). Press Parallel and Same line twice to see the other two.

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.text: Stack the numbers into a matrix and the system becomes one line, Ax = b:  \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{A} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}}_{x} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}}_{b}  Read by rows , it's the two lines above. Read by columns , it's chapter 1's picture: "x of the first column plus y of the second must land on b". Which mix of the arrows (1, 3) and (2, 1) reaches the yellow target (7, 11)? Turn the knobs: x (coffees) y (bagels) The column picture explains when there's an answer. If the two columns point in different directions, mixing them reaches every point of the plane, so every b has exactly one recipe. If they lie on one line, mixes of them stay on that line: a b off it is unreachable, and a b on it has endless recipes. And "columns on one line" is exactly chapter 1's determinant zero : the matrix squashes the plane flat. Ax = b asks which mix of A's columns lands on b. Columns pointing in different directions reach everywhere, each spot by exactly one mix; columns on one line reach only that line. The picture Rows: lines that must all pass through the answer. Columns: arrows you mix to land on the target. The math \det A = a d - b c \neq 0: exactly one solution, for every b. \det A = 0: none or infinitely many, depending on b. The matrix is then called singular .

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.section: 3. Dependence and rank: how many equations really count
sections.text: Add a third sentence: "four coffees and three bagels cost $18". Is that new information? No: it's the first two receipts added together, (x + 2y) + (3x + y) = 7 + 11. An equation that's a mix of others is linearly dependent on them: it can be true (and then it adds nothing) or contradict them (and then there's no answer), but it can never pin down anything new. The rank of a matrix counts the equations that really count: the most rows you can pick with none being a mix of the others. Remarkably, it's always the same as the most independent columns . In the column picture, rank is the dimension of everywhere Ax can reach: a point (rank 0), a line (rank 1), the plane (rank 2), and so on. Why an ML engineer cares: a dataset is a matrix, one row per example, one column per feature. If one column is a mix of others (price in dollars and price in cents, or "rooms" alongside "bedrooms + other rooms"), the matrix loses rank and a linear model's knobs stop having one best value: you can shift weight between the twin columns forever without changing a single prediction. And when Part 4 fine-tunes a big model with LoRA , it's betting the change it needs is low rank : a huge matrix of updates built from a few independent columns.

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.text: With three unknowns, each equation is a plane in 3D and drawing stops helping. What a computer does instead is Gaussian elimination : use the first equation to remove x from all the others, then the new second to remove y from the ones below, and so on, until the last row has one unknown. Then solve from the bottom up. The only moves allowed are ones that keep the answers the same: subtract a multiple of one row from another, or swap two rows. system one answer a repeated equation a contradiction Next step Start over Here's elimination as code, written the way libraries do it: before each step it swaps up the row with the biggest number in the current column ( partial pivoting ), because dividing by a tiny pivot magnifies rounding errors. Elimination on n unknowns takes about n^3/3 multiplications: a thousand unknowns is a third of a billion, a fraction of a second. That cube is why, for millions of unknowns (a neural network's weights), nobody solves equations: gradient descent takes cheap steps instead.

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.text: The identity matrix I has 1s down the diagonal and 0s elsewhere: it's the move that doesn't move anything, Iv = v. The inverse A^{-1} is the move that undoes A: A^{-1} A = A A^{-1} = I. If you had it, solving would be one multiplication: x = A^{-1} b. Drag the columns of A ( green and red , as in chapter 1). The dashed arrows are the columns of A^{-1}, the move that puts the grid back. Then press Nearly flat . Reset Nearly flat Flat The inverse undoes a move, and exists only if nothing was squashed. Dividing by the determinant is the price of undoing: a nearly flat matrix makes small errors huge. A practical rule: in code, almost never compute an inverse just to solve Ax = b. Elimination is faster and loses less to rounding. In NumPy that's np.linalg.solve(A, b) , not np.linalg.inv(A) @ b .

sections.lesson: Systems of equations, rank and inverses
sections.section: 6. Linear regression with no training loop
sections.text: Start 2's six taxi rides give six equations for two knobs, a \cdot \text{km} + b = \text{minutes}, one per ride. Six lines through a two-knob plane don't meet in one point: there's no exact answer . Least squares asks for the next best thing, the (a, b) with the smallest squared error. Its gradient (Calculus 2) is zero exactly where  X^\top X \, w = X^\top y  with X the rides' table (a column of km and a column of 1s), y the minutes, w = (a, b). These are the normal equations : always a square system, 2 equations for 2 knobs here, which our solve handles in one go. Least squares finds the reachable point Xw closest to y, and closest means the leftover error is perpendicular to everything reachable. So why does ML bother with gradient descent? Because this only works when the error is a bowl (a linear model with squared error), and only while X^\top X is small enough to eliminate: with n features it's n \times n, and the cost grows like n^3. A network bends its inputs (chapter 1's ReLU), its error isn't a simple bowl, and it has millions of knobs. Gradient descent works for all of it.

sections.section: 1. A slope is "how much does it change?"
sections.text: Here's a bumpy curve. The yellow line joins your point to another point a step h to the right: it rises some amount over a run of h . Drag the blue point along the curve, and shrink h . step h As h shrinks, the line stops cutting the curve and just touches it: that's the tangent , and its slope is the derivative . Zoom in on any smooth curve far enough and it looks straight; the derivative is the slope of that straight bit. Positive means "going up to the right", negative means "going down", zero means you're at a flat spot: the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley. The picture The slope of the line that just touches the curve: how many units it rises per unit you walk right. The math f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}: rise over run, with the run shrunk to nothing. For simple functions the limit can be worked out once, by hand, and gives rules you can reuse. Take f(x) = x^2:  \frac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h} = \frac{x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2}{h} = 2x + h \;\xrightarrow{\;h \to 0\;}\; 2x  So the slope of x^2 at any x is 2x. The same algebra gives the rules every library uses: (x^n)' = n x^{n-1}, (e^x)' = e^x, (\ln x)' = 1/x, and slopes of sums add up. A computer can also skip the algebra and just try a small h, which is what the code below does. Watch what happens when h gets too small.

Say the curve measures how wrong we are, and we want the lowest point. We can't see the whole curve (in a real network it lives in a million dimensions), but we can always measure the slope where we stand. So: take a step against the slope . If the ground tilts up to the right, step left. Repeat. x ← x − (learning rate) × slope Step Roll Drop somewhere else learning rate 0.15 Play with the learning rate. Small, and the ball crawls. Big, and it overshoots, bouncing from wall to wall, or flies off entirely. Drop it on the right and it settles in the shallow valley , never finding the deeper one: gradient descent only knows the ground under its feet. Choosing the step size, and getting out of shallow valleys, is half the craft of training networks. Gradient descent only feels the ground under its feet: step against the slope, with steps small enough for how sharply the valley curves.

sections.section: 3. Two inputs: the gradient is an arrow
sections.text: Now the "wrongness" depends on two numbers, so it's a landscape, drawn here like a map: dark is low, bright is high, and the lines are contours of equal height. At any spot you can ask two questions: how steep is it going right, and how steep going up? Those two slopes together make an arrow, the gradient . Drag the point. The red arrow (the gradient) always points straight uphill, the steepest way up, and it's always perpendicular to the contour line you're standing on. Its length says how steep. The green arrow is the opposite: steepest downhill. That's the direction gradient descent walks. The gradient is an arrow that points the steepest way uphill, and its length says how steep. Walking against it is the fastest way down, for a small enough step.

Here's the whole idea of training, in miniature. On the left: some points, and a line y = w·x + b that should fit them. How wrong the line is (the average squared vertical miss, called the loss ) depends on two numbers, w and b . On the right: that loss as a landscape over every possible (w, b) . Each training step is one step downhill on the right, and the line on the left gets better. Train One step New points Start over learning rate 0.05 Drag the points on the left and the landscape on the right reshapes itself: the loss depends on the data. Drag the yellow dot on the right to start the line somewhere else. A real network is this exact loop with millions of numbers instead of two: measure the loss, compute its gradient, step downhill, repeat. The only hard part left is computing the gradient for millions of numbers at once, efficiently. That's backpropagation , and it's coming up right after we build a single neuron . Training is this loop: measure the loss, find its gradient with respect to every knob, take a step downhill, repeat. Inspired by 3Blue1Brown's gradient descent and Essence of Calculus . All lessons: AI from scratch .

sections.section: 1. Zoom in until the curve is a line
sections.text: Pick a point a on a curve and a second point a distance h further along. The red line through both has slope "rise over run". Shrink h: the red line turns into the green tangent , the line the curve looks like if you zoom in far enough. Its slope is the derivative .  f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}  f(x) = x² x³ − x sin x eˣ a h Notice the gap between the two slopes shrinks in step with h: halve h, halve the gap. For x^2 you can see why: \frac{(a+h)^2 - a^2}{h} = \frac{2ah + h^2}{h} = 2a + h. Let h go to zero and what's left is 2a. A derivative is also a sensitivity : near a, f(a + \Delta) \approx f(a) + f'(a)\,\Delta. If the loss has derivative 6 with respect to a weight, nudging that weight up by 0.001 raises the loss by about 0.006. Gradient descent (chapter 2) is just this sentence used backwards. Zoom in far enough and a smooth curve looks like a straight line; the derivative is that line's slope, and it says how much the output moves per unit you move the input.

Nobody takes limits by hand. Every function a network computes is built from a few pieces, and each piece has a rule: function derivative in words c 0 a constant doesn't change x^n n x^{n-1} power rule (works for n = -1, \tfrac12, any n) c\,f + g c\,f' + g' derivatives add and scale f \cdot g f' g + f g' product rule: each one changes while the other holds f(g(x)) f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x) chain rule: multiply the slopes along the way e^x e^x its own slope (section 3) \ln x 1/x the log flattens as it grows Plus \sin' = \cos and \cos' = -\sin for waves. Two worked examples: \frac{d}{dx}\, x^2 \sin x = 2x \sin x + x^2 \cos x (product rule), and the bell curve \frac{d}{dx}\, e^{-x^2} = e^{-x^2} \cdot (-2x) (chain rule: outside slope times inside slope). The chain rule is the one that matters most: a network is a long chain of functions, and backprop (chapter 4) is the chain rule run from the loss backwards. The chain rule multiplies the slopes along the way, and a network is one long chain.

sections.section: 3. ex and ln: the two functions ML is made of
sections.text: e^x is the function that grows at a rate equal to its size: its slope everywhere is its own value. That makes it the natural way to turn any score into something positive with a clean derivative, which is exactly what softmax does (chapter 5). Its inverse, \ln x, has slope 1/x: steep near zero, flat for large x. Logs are everywhere in ML for two reasons. First, \ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b: the probability of a whole sentence is a product of a thousand token probabilities, and the log turns it into a sum, which has a far easier derivative. Second, the product doesn't fit in a computer: The loss for a prediction is -\ln p, where p is the probability the model gave the right answer. Its derivative is -1/p: when the model is confidently wrong (tiny p), the slope is huge and the correction is strong.

Between layers, a network bends its numbers with an activation function. Backprop multiplies by the activation's derivative at every layer, so its shape decides whether learning signals survive the trip. Blue is the function, yellow its derivative. activation sigmoid σ tanh ReLU softplus GELU x The sigmoid \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} has a neat derivative, \sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)\,(1 - \sigma(x)), and it is never more than 0.25. Stack ten sigmoid layers and the chain rule multiplies ten of those slopes together: the signal reaching the first layer is at most 0.25^{10}, about one millionth. That's the vanishing gradient that stalled deep networks for years. ReLU (slope exactly 1 for positive inputs) fixed most of it; its weakness is slope 0 for negative inputs, where a neuron can "die" and never recover. GELU, used in transformers, is a smooth ReLU. Backprop multiplies one activation slope per layer, so an activation whose slope is usually far below 1 starves the early layers.

sections.section: 5. Derivatives by computer, and checking them
sections.text: A computer can estimate a slope straight from the definition with a small h: the forward difference \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}, or the more accurate central difference \frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}. Smaller h should be better. Here is the actual error for f = \sin at x = 1, on a log scale (each grid line is ten times more): h = 10^ forward difference central difference Going right to left, both errors fall as h shrinks (forward like h, central like h^2), then turn around and climb. Below about h = 10^{-8}, f(x+h) and f(x) agree in almost all of their 16 digits, and subtracting them leaves mostly rounding noise, which is then divided by a tiny h. Floating point puts a floor under how precisely you can measure a slope this way. Why not train with numerical derivatives? They cost one or two extra evaluations of the whole network per parameter : a billion-parameter model would need two billion forward passes for one step. Backprop gets every derivative for about the cost of two or three forward passes. So engineers use numerical derivatives for one job: gradient checking , comparing them against the hand-derived or backprop gradient on a few inputs to catch bugs.

Here is f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + 2y^2 seen from above: brighter is higher, and each band is one unit of height, so band edges are contour lines . Drag the yellow point . Freeze y and walk in x: the slope you feel is the partial derivative \partial f/\partial x, computed by treating y as a constant. Same for y.   rac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x + y, \qquad  rac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x + 4y, \qquad 
abla f =  egin{pmatrix} 2x + y \ x + 4y \end{pmatrix}  direction θ gradient ∇f your direction u along the contour Stack the partials into a vector and you get the gradient 
abla f. Walk in any direction u (a unit vector) and your slope is the directional derivative

That's why the gradient always crosses contour lines at right angles, and why "step against the gradient" is the fastest way down. A partial derivative is a slope with everything else frozen. Stacked, they make the gradient, and the slope in any direction is the gradient dotted with that direction.

sections.section: 2. The gradients you'll meet every day
sections.text:
In ML the inputs are vectors and matrices, and a handful of gradients cover nearly everything. Each can be checked one partial at a time, like section 1: function (a number) gradient why w \cdot x

The data comes from y = 1 + 3x_1 - 2x_2 plus noise; the first column of X is all ones, so w_0 is the bias.

sections.section: 3. The Jacobian: a matrix for every point
sections.text: Chapter 1 showed a matrix as a move of the whole plane that keeps grid lines straight. A layer with a nonlinearity bends them. Below, F(x, y) = (x + 0.4\sin 1.5y,\; y + 0.4\sin 1.5x) warps the grid. But zoom in on any point and the bend disappears: near a point, every smooth map looks like a matrix . That matrix is the Jacobian , the table of every output's partial with respect to every input:  J = \begin{pmatrix} \partial F_1/\partial x & \partial F_1/\partial y \\ \partial F_2/\partial x & \partial F_2/\partial y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.6\cos 1.5y \\ 0.6\cos 1.5x & 1 \end{pmatrix}  square side the square (drag it) where F sends it where J predicts Shrink the square: the yellow curved patch and the red parallelogram become the same shape, the 2D version of the secant turning into the tangent. And just as in chapter 1, the Jacobian's determinant is the local area scale: the patch's area divided by the square's tends to \det J. That fact comes back in Calculus 4, when a change of variables has to keep a probability's total area at 1. Near any point, a smooth map is a matrix: its Jacobian. The Jacobian's determinant is how much the map scales small areas there.

Roll two dice. There are 36 equally likely outcomes, one per square below (across: the first die, up: the second). When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just  P(A) = \frac{\text{outcomes in } A}{\text{all outcomes}}  Pick two events. Squares only in A are blue , only in B red , in both yellow . A: B: Three rules fall straight out of counting: rule formula why Complement P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A) every square is either in A or not Sum rule P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) adding counts the yellow squares twice, so take them off once Independence P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) only when knowing one tells you nothing about the other, like two separate dice

How many people must be in a room before it's more likely than not that two share a birthday? Most people guess around 180. A car is behind one of three doors, goats behind the other two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door with a goat, and offers you a switch. Should you? "Given that B happened" means: throw away every outcome where it didn't, and count again inside what's left.  P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}  Read the bar as "given". Here's the same dice square, with the outcomes outside B dimmed: A: given B: Two events are independent exactly when conditioning changes nothing: P(A \mid B) = P(A). Try "a double" given "first die is 6": still 1/6. Every classifier in this course is a conditional probability: P(\text{cat} \mid \text{these pixels}). Conditioning is shrinking the world to what you now know, and counting again inside it.

sections.section: 4. Bayes' rule: turning a probability around
sections.text: A test for a disease catches 90% of people who have it (its sensitivity ) and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people (its false positive rate ). One person in a hundred has the disease. You test positive. How worried should you be? Here are 1000 people: red have the disease, grey don't, and a bright dot means a positive test. have the disease sensitivity false positives Count the bright dots: most of them are grey. Ten people are sick and 9 of them test positive, but 990 are healthy and 9% of them, about 89, test positive too. A positive test means you're one of about 98 bright dots, and only 9 of those are red: about 9%. That's Bayes' rule :  P(\text{sick} \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid \text{sick})\, P(\text{sick})}{P(+)} = \frac{0.9 \times 0.01}{0.9 \times 0.01 + 0.09 \times 0.99} \approx 0.092  The picture Keep only the bright dots (the evidence happened). The answer is the red share of them. The math P(H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}: the prior P(H) times the likelihood P(E \mid H), divided by how common the evidence is overall. The result is the posterior . Bayes: what you believe after the evidence is what you believed before, times how well each explanation predicted that evidence, rescaled to add up to 1.

sections.section: 5. A spam filter from Bayes' rule
sections.text: Turn it around for email: P(\text{spam} \mid \text{words}). Bayes says that's proportional to P(\text{spam}) \cdot P(\text{words} \mid \text{spam}), and the "naive" part assumes words appear independently given the class, so the likelihood is a product over words:  P(\text{spam} \mid w_1 \dots w_k) \;\propto\; P(\text{spam}) \prod_{i=1}^{k} P(w_i \mid \text{spam})  Each P(w \mid \text{spam}) is counted from examples: how often the word appears in spam. Two practical tricks from the math warm-up: add 1 to every count (so an unseen word doesn't zero out the whole product), and add logs instead of multiplying (so long emails don't underflow). The independence assumption is plainly false ("free" and "prize" go together) yet the filter works well, which is a theme in ML: a wrong model can still be a useful one.

sections.section: 6. Distributions: every value's probability at once
sections.text: A random variable is a number that comes out of a random process: the sum of two dice, the number of heads in 10 flips. Its distribution says how likely each value is. Three you'll meet constantly: Bernoulli(p) : one yes/no trial, 1 with probability p, else 0. A click, a fraud, a correct prediction. Binomial(n, p) : the number of yeses in n independent Bernoulli trials. P(k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}, where \binom{n}{k} ("n choose k") counts the orders the k yeses could come in. Uniform : every value in a range equally likely. Math.random() is uniform between 0 and 1. Below, the bars are the binomial's PMF (probability mass function: the probability of each exact value) and the green steps its CDF (cumulative distribution function: the probability of that value or less , a running sum of the bars). trials n chance p For values that can be anything in a range (a time, a height), single exact values have probability zero, so a PDF (density) replaces the bars, and probability is area under it (Calculus 4). The CDF works the same for both: it climbs from 0 to 1, and P(a

A computer only makes uniform random numbers. To get waiting times for a train that comes on average every 4 minutes (an exponential distribution, CDF F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/4}), use the CDF backwards: pick a uniform u between 0 and 1 on the up axis, go across until you hit the CDF, and drop down. That x is your sample. Steep parts of the CDF catch many u's, so values land there often. Draw 1 Draw 500 Clear A distribution gives every value's probability; its CDF, read backwards, turns uniform random numbers into samples of it.

Each dot is one outage, placed by how many hours it lasted (shaken up and down a little so they don't hide each other). The yellow line is the mean , the plain average. The blue line is the median , the middle value: half the outages were shorter, half longer. log scale Add one 2000-hour outage On the plain scale almost everything is squashed against the left edge by a few outages that lasted weeks. The mean, 8.2 hours, sits where hardly any outage is. The median, 1.6 hours, is what a rider actually meets. Press Add one : a single extreme value drags the mean up by hours while the median barely moves. The median is robust : outliers can't push it around.  \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \qquad \text{median} = \text{the middle value after sorting}  The mode is the most common value. It's most useful for categories: here the most common reason is "Under Investigation". The median is what a typical case looks like; the mean is what totals need. On lopsided data they disagree, and each answers a different question.

sections.section: 2. How spread out: variance and standard deviation
sections.text: Two datasets can share a mean and still look nothing alike. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation \sigma is its square root, which brings it back to the data's units:  \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}  (When you estimate the spread of a whole population from a sample, you divide by n - 1 instead; Probability 3 explains why. With hundreds of points the difference is tiny.) Squaring makes big deviations count a lot, so like the mean, the standard deviation is easily blown up by outliers: for our outages it's 56 hours, wider than nearly every outage. Standardizing turns any value into "how many standard deviations from the mean": the z-score z = (x - \bar{x}) / \sigma. After it, every feature has mean 0 and spread 1. That's exactly the feature scaling models need: Calculus 3 showed gradient descent zigzagging in a stretched valley, and putting all features on the same scale is what un-stretches it. The standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean, and a z-score measures any value in those units, which puts every feature on one scale.

The median splits the data in half. Quantiles split it anywhere: the 25th percentile (first quartile, Q1) has a quarter of the data below it, the 75th (Q3) three quarters. The interquartile range IQR = Q3 − Q1 is the spread of the middle half, and like the median, outliers can't touch it. A box plot draws exactly that: the box runs from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, the whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 IQR of the box, and anything beyond is drawn on its own as a possible outlier. The faint shape behind each box is a violin : the same data's density (section 4), mirrored. Here are elevators and escalators side by side, on a log scale:

sections.section: 4. The shape: histograms and density estimates
sections.text: A histogram cuts the range into bins and counts the points in each. Its look depends a lot on the bin width you pick. A kernel density estimate (KDE) instead puts a small bell curve on every point and adds them up, giving a smooth estimate of the density (Calculus 4). Its knob is the bandwidth , the width of each little bell. The x-axis here is \log_{10} of hours: 0 is 1 hour, 1 is 10 hours, 2 is 100. bins bandwidth On the log scale the shape is a single hump, leaning a little right. On the plain scale it's wildly skewed : a big pile near zero and a long tail to the right. Skewness measures that lopsidedness (0 for symmetric, positive for a long right tail), and kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are compared with a bell curve. Durations, prices, incomes and file sizes are all right-skewed, and taking logs is the standard fix: models (and averages) behave much better on \log x than on x.

sections.section: 5. Is it a bell curve? The QQ plot
sections.text: Many methods assume data is roughly normal (a bell curve). To check, sort the data, standardize it, and plot each point against where it would be if the data were perfectly normal: the matching quantile of the bell curve. Normal data falls on the diagonal; skew bends it away. take logs first

With two variables at once, count every combination. This is the joint table of kind × "fixed within 2 hours?". The totals in the margins are the marginal counts: each variable on its own, ignoring the other. A conditional distribution picks one row and divides by its total: "of the elevator outages, what share ran over 2 hours?". That's Probability 1's P(A \mid B), counted from real data.

For each outage the MTA posts an estimated return time. Does the estimate predict how long it actually takes? Each dot is one outage: across is the estimate, up is the truth. log scale Covariance measures whether two variables move together: the average of (x's distance from its mean) times (y's distance from its mean). When both are above or both below their means, the product is positive. Correlation r divides by both standard deviations, which pins it between −1 (a perfect falling line) and +1 (a perfect rising line), with 0 meaning no straight-line relation:  \operatorname{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}), \qquad r = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(x, y)}{\sigma_x \sigma_y}  A correlation is also just the mean product of z-scores: standardize both, multiply pairwise, average. Correlation is the average product of z-scores: how consistently two things sit on the same side of their means, along a straight line. Two more warnings. Correlation only sees straight-line relations: points on a perfect circle have r = 0. And correlation isn't causation: elevator outages correlate with longer estimates and longer durations, but the estimate doesn't cause the repair to take longer; the kind of breakdown drives both.

The bell curve has a version for several variables at once, the multivariate normal . In 2D it's a hill whose contour lines are ellipses. It's described by the two means and a covariance matrix : each variable's variance on the diagonal, their covariance off it:  \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_x^2 & \rho\,\sigma_x \sigma_y \\ \rho\,\sigma_x \sigma_y & \sigma_y^2 \end{pmatrix}  Shape it: the dots are 600 samples, the rings are 1 and 2 standard deviations. σx σy correlation ρ The ellipse's long axis is the direction the data varies most, and finding those axes is exactly what PCA does, using the covariance matrix's eigenvectors (Linear algebra 2). The same shape shows up as the Gaussian anomaly detector in stage 3: points outside the outer ring are rare.

sections.section: 1. A basis is a choice of steps
sections.text: Chapter 1 described every point with two steps, \hat\imath = (1, 0) and \hat\jmath = (0, 1). Nothing forces that choice. Any two arrows that don't lie on one line can reach every point of the plane by mixing them (their span is the whole plane), so they form a basis , and a point's coordinates are just how much of each step you take. Linear algebra 1's column picture was this exact question.

sections.section: 2. The arrows a matrix only stretches
sections.text: Drag the blue arrow v. The yellow arrow is where the matrix sends it, Av. Usually it points somewhere else. Find the directions where yellow lies exactly along blue: there Av = \lambda v for some number \lambda, the eigenvalue , and v is an eigenvector . The dashed lines show where they are once you've looked. matrix [2 1; 1 2] stretch [3 1; 0 2] [1 2; 2 1] [1 1; 0 1] shear [0 −1; 1 0] rotate show the eigen-directions Apply A over and over Eigenvectors are the directions a matrix only stretches, never turns; the eigenvalue is how much it stretches them.

Av = \lambda v means (A - \lambda I)v = 0 for a nonzero v: the matrix A - \lambda I squashes some arrow to zero, so it must be singular, which means its determinant is zero (Linear algebra 1). That gives an equation for \lambda alone:

sections.section: 4. Repeat a move, and the biggest eigenvalue wins
sections.text: Press Apply A over and over above. Each press of the move stretches the part of v along each eigenvector by its own \lambda. After k moves that's \lambda^k: the part along the biggest eigenvalue grows fastest and takes over, so the arrow swings onto the dominant eigenvector . That's power iteration , the simplest way to find an eigenvector: multiply, rescale, repeat.  v = c_1 e_1 + c_2 e_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad A^k v = c_1 \lambda_1^k e_1 + c_2 \lambda_2^k e_2  How fast it lines up depends on the ratio |\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|: the second part shrinks by that factor every step. Writing a matrix in its own eigenbasis, A = V \Lambda V^{-1} with the eigenvalues on the diagonal of \Lambda, turns "apply it k times" into "raise each eigenvalue to the k": A^k = V \Lambda^k V^{-1}. Repeat a move and the direction with the biggest stretch takes over; how fast depends on how far ahead the winner is.

sections.section: 5. A random walk over this site: PageRank
sections.text: Imagine a reader who clicks random links on this site forever. Which pages do they spend the most time on? Put everyone on one page, then each step, each page shares its readers equally among the pages it links to. That's a matrix times a vector, repeated: a Markov chain . This is the real link graph of this site's 169 pages (as of 12 October 2026). Everyone starts on the last ham radio lesson. 1 step 10 steps Start over The shares settle into a fixed list no matter where the readers started. That fixed point is a vector r with Mr = r: an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1, and that's PageRank , the idea Google was founded on. One fix makes it work: with probability 0.15 each step, a reader gets bored and jumps to a random page (the damping ). Without it, readers could get stuck in a corner of pages that only link to each other, and the answer would depend on where they started.

sections.section: 6. Projection: the shadow on a line
sections.text: To project a point onto a line through the origin with direction u (length 1), drop a perpendicular: the shadow is (x \cdot u)\,u, and the number x \cdot u is the point's coordinate along that line. The leftover, x - (x \cdot u)u, is at right angles to u, so by Pythagoras, length² of x = shadow² + leftover².

sections.section: 7. PCA: the direction your data cares about most
sections.text: Back to Probability 2's outages: each dot is one outage, across the MTA's estimate, up the actual time, both as \log_{10} hours with the mean subtracted. Turn the line. Each dot casts a shadow on it, and the red sticks are what the line misses. Find the angle where the shadows spread out the most. angle Let PCA find it Two goals turn out to be one. Spreading the shadows as wide as possible and making the red sticks as short as possible are the same thing, because shadow² + stick² is fixed for every dot (Pythagoras again). And the best direction is no search at all: the variance along a unit direction u is u^\top \Sigma u, with \Sigma the covariance matrix from Probability 2, and that's largest exactly along \Sigma's top eigenvector , with the eigenvalue as the variance captured. That's principal component analysis : Subtract the mean of every feature (often also divide by its standard deviation). Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma. Its eigenvectors, sorted by eigenvalue, are the principal components; each eigenvalue is how much variance that direction holds. Keep the top few and describe every example by its coordinates along them. PCA turns the data to its own best axes: the first is the direction of greatest spread, and each eigenvalue says how much of the spread its direction holds. In 2D that's a curiosity. With a 28×28 image (784 numbers) or a word embedding (768), it's how you compress, denoise, and plot data you can't see: a few components often hold most of the variance. PCA is also the first thing to try for visualizing embeddings in stage 6. Its limit: it only f

Calculus 3's Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, is symmetric, so it has eigenvectors at right angles. They're the valley's main axes, and each eigenvalue is the curvature along its axis. The condition number \lambda_{\max} / \lambda_{\min} is how stretched the valley is, and why gradient descent zigzags: the learning rate must stay under 2/\lambda_{\max}, so the flattest direction crawls along at a speed set by \lambda_{\min}/\lambda_{\max}. Standardizing features (Probability 2) and PCA whitening (rotate onto the components, then divide each by its standard deviation) both push those eigenvalues toward equal, which is why scaled inputs train faster. The Hessian's eigenvalues are the valley's curvatures along its main axes; their ratio, the condition number, sets how slowly gradient descent crawls.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.section: 1. Every matrix turns a circle into an ellipse
sections.text: Drag the blue and yellow arrows: they're where the matrix sends the steps \hat\imath and \hat\jmath (chapter 1). The gray circle of unit arrows becomes a tilted ellipse, always. Its longest radius is the most the matrix stretches anything, its shortest the least. The green and pink arrows are the two unit arrows that land exactly on the ellipse's axes. Now press Play : the same matrix as three simple moves. Play the three moves move  A = U\,\Sigma\,V^\top \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge 0  Read it right to left, like a sequence of moves: V^\top rotates the plane so the two directions that will become the ellipse's axes (the columns of V, the right singular vectors ) lie along x and y; \Sigma stretches x by \sigma_1 and y by \sigma_2, the singular values ; U rotates the result into place, its columns pointing along the ellipse's axes. (When the matrix flips the plane over, one stretch is shown negative.) In more dimensions it's the same: an m \times n matrix rotates, stretches along up to \min(m, n) axes, and rotates again. Every matrix, whatever it does, is a rotation, a stretch along two perpendicular axes, and another rotation: the circle always becomes an ellipse.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.text: For a symmetric matrix (a covariance, a Hessian), the two ideas meet: singular values are the eigenvalues' sizes, and U and V are the eigenvectors. For other matrices they differ, and the SVD still exists when eigenvectors don't (a shear has only one eigen-direction, but its circle still becomes an ellipse). The link that always holds: A^\top A is symmetric, its eigenvalues are \sigma_i^2, and its eigenvectors are V. The ratio \sigma_1/\sigma_2 is linear algebra 1's condition number : how stretched the ellipse is, and how much rounding errors get magnified when you solve with this matrix. Eigenvalues tell you what happens if you apply a matrix over and over; singular values tell you the most and least it can stretch anything in one go.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.text: Written as a sum, the SVD is a stack of simple layers, each a column times a row, weighted by its singular value:  A = \sigma_1 u_1 v_1^\top + \sigma_2 u_2 v_2^\top + \dots  Each layer u_i v_i^\top is a rank-1 matrix (every row a multiple of the same row). Keep only the k biggest and you have the best possible rank-k approximation of A: no other choice of k layers comes closer (the Eckart–Young theorem). A grayscale photo is a matrix of brightnesses, so here is Grace Hopper, the computing pioneer, in 1984 (U.S. Navy photo, public domain), rebuilt from her first few layers: A matrix is a stack of layers, biggest first; dropping the small ones loses the least.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.text: Linear algebra 2 found principal components as eigenvectors of the covariance matrix X^\top X/(n-1) of centered data. The SVD of the centered data itself gives the same directions without ever forming X^\top X (which squares the condition number, and loses precision): the rows of V^\top are the components, and \sigma_i^2/(n-1) are the variances along them. This is how scikit-learn's PCA does it.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.text: Eight people rated ten films, 1 to 5 stars, but 30% of the ratings are missing. The table is made up from two hidden tastes (how much each film is an action film or a love story, how much each person likes each), plus noise. Nobody tells the SVD that; it finds two big singular values and much smaller ones after them. To guess the missing ratings: fill them with each film's average, take the rank-2 version, put its guesses into the gaps, and repeat. This is the idea behind the Netflix Prize-era recommenders, and still behind many today. The directions the SVD finds are mixtures you name afterwards ("taste 1 is mostly action against romance"). Real recommenders add regularization and learn from millions of ratings, but the shape of the answer is this one: a person is a short vector of tastes, a film is a short vector of qualities, and a rating is roughly their dot product. If a few hidden factors explain a table, the table is close to low rank, and its biggest layers are those factors.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.text: Linear algebra 1 solved square, invertible systems, and noted that np.linalg.lstsq "uses an SVD". Here's why: invert each stretch, \sigma_i \to 1/\sigma_i, and skip the ones that are zero (or tiny). That's the pseudo-inverse A^+ = V\,\Sigma^+\,U^\top. It exists for every matrix; for an overdetermined system it gives the least-squares answer, and when columns repeat (linear algebra 1's twin column) it still gives one sensible answer, the smallest weights that fit. Turn the problem so the matrix is just stretches, divide by each stretch you can, and leave the rest alone.

sections.lesson: Singular value decomposition: rotate, stretch, rotate
sections.section: 7. Why big models fine-tune with low rank
sections.text: A large language model's layer can be a 4,096 × 4,096 matrix: 16.8 million weights. Fine-tuning it for a new task changes those weights by some \Delta W, and experiments found that useful changes are close to low-rank: a few directions matter. LoRA (stage 6) trains the change directly as a product \Delta W = B A with B of shape 4,096 × r and A of shape r × 4,096, for a small rank r like 8. That's the SVD's lesson used in reverse: if only a few layers matter, learn only those.

sections.section: 1. A weighted sum and a bend
sections.text: Our neuron looks at a point with two numbers, (x₁, x₂) . It computes z = w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ + b   →   output = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e −z ) The bend σ (the sigmoid) squashes any number into 0…1, so the output reads like "how sure am I that this point is blue ?". The two weights form an arrow, w . Drag its tip , slide the bias, and drag the green probe point . bias b 0 Look at the shading: the neuron splits the plane with a straight line, where z = 0 and it's exactly 50% sure. That line is always perpendicular to the weight arrow . The arrow points toward "more blue", its length says how sharp the switch is (a long arrow means a crisp edge, a short one a fuzzy blur), and the bias slides the line back and forth without turning it. Remember chapter 1: w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ is a matrix with one row. A neuron is a tiny layer. A neuron draws one straight line across its inputs and reports how far past the line a point is, squashed into a probability.

Here are two clouds of points. We want the neuron to say "blue" for blue points and "red" for red ones. Its loss (how wrong it is) is the log loss : for each point, how surprised the neuron is by the right answer. Training is chapter 2's loop: compute the gradient of the loss with respect to w₁, w₂, b , step downhill, repeat. Train Forget everything New clouds Drag points around · click empty space to add a blue point, shift-click (or long-press) for red Notice what the gradient does here, in plain words: every misclassified point pulls the line toward itself and pushes the weight arrow toward its own side. Points the neuron already gets right, with confidence, barely pull at all. That's the whole of learning for one neuron: lots of small nudges from its mistakes. Learning is many small nudges: each point pulls by how wrong it is, \hat p - y, so mistakes teach and confident right answers barely matter.

Now a pattern a child can see: blue in two opposite corners, red in the other two (it's called XOR ). Train the single neuron on it. Train one neuron Train a hidden layer (4 neurons) Reset It can't. However it turns its line, one straight cut can't put opposite corners together, so it gets stuck around half right. This exact problem stalled neural network research for a decade in the 1970s. The fix is the one from chapter 1: stack layers . Four neurons in a hidden layer each make their own cut; a final neuron combines their answers, and now the boundary can bend around the corners. Press the second button and watch it curve. One neuron can only cut with a straight line. A hidden layer moves the points to new positions where a straight cut works. But how did that hidden layer learn? Each of its neurons had to figure out its share of the blame for the final answer, through the neuron after it. Passing blame backwards like that is backpropagation : the next chapter. All chapters: AI from scratch . Inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Neural Networks series.

Three machines in a row: the first triples its input, the second adds 2, the third squares. Nudge x a little and watch the nudge travel. x 0.50 nudge Δx 0.050 Each machine stretches the nudge by its own slope: ×3, then ×1, then ×2·(its input). The final nudge is the product of all three, so the derivative of the whole chain is the product of the local slopes . That's the chain rule. Notice we can compute it either way: start at x and multiply forward, or start at the end and multiply backward. Backward turns out to be the magic trick. The picture Each machine stretches a small nudge by its own slope. Stretches multiply. The math The chain rule: for c(b(a(x))), \dfrac{dc}{dx} = \dfrac{dc}{db} \cdot \dfrac{db}{da} \cdot \dfrac{da}{dx}. A small nudge travels down a chain, stretched by each link's slope along the way; the stretches multiply.

sections.section: 2. A tiny network, forward and backward
sections.text: Here's one neuron feeding another, computing a prediction ŷ for an input x = 1.5 , and the loss: how far ŷ is from the target y = 0.8 , squared. Dashed boxes are the weights we can change. Press Forward to compute values left to right, then Backward to pass blame right to left. Forward Backward Step downhill Train 50 steps Reset Read the red numbers right to left. The loss starts with blame 1 (it's what we measure). Each node hands blame to the nodes it came from, multiplied by the local slope on the arrow between them: how much it moves when that input moves. A node used twice would add up the blame from both uses. When the pass reaches a weight, its red number is exactly ∂loss/∂weight : chapter 2's gradient. "Step downhill" moves every weight against its gradient, and the next forward pass has a smaller loss. Backprop passes blame from right to left: each node multiplies the blame it receives by its own local slope and hands it on, and blame arriving from several uses adds up.

sections.section: 3. Did backprop get it right? Nudge and see
sections.text: The slow, obvious way to get a gradient: nudge one weight by a tiny ε, rerun the forward pass, and see how much the loss changed. Real libraries use this as a test. Check by nudging each weight

sections.section: 4. Why this is the trick that made deep learning
sections.text: Nudging works, but it needs one extra forward pass per weight . Backprop gets every gradient from one forward and one backward pass, about the cost of three forward passes, however many weights there are. weights in the network That gap is why networks with billions of weights can be trained at all. Everything since, convolutions for images and attention for language, is new shapes of graphs with the same forward and backward passes running through them. Coming up on the path: what the loss should actually be when a network has to choose between answers, probability and loss . All chapters: AI from scratch . Inspired by 3Blue1Brown's Backpropagation calculus and Andrej Karpathy's micrograd.

Calculus 2 introduced the Jacobian, the matrix of every output's slope with respect to every input. In that language the whole backward pass is one line. A network is a chain: x \to h_1 \to h_2 \to \dots \to L. The multivariable chain rule says the Jacobian of a chain is the product of the Jacobians of its links:  \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial h_k}}_{1 \times m} \; \underbrace{\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}}_{m \times m} \cdots \underbrace{\frac{\partial h_1}{\partial x}}_{m \times n}  Matrix products are associative, so you can multiply in either order and get the same answer, but not for the same price. The loss is one number, so the leftmost factor is a single row. Multiply left to right and every step is a row times a matrix: a vector-Jacobian product , about m^2 work, and the result is still one row. That is reverse mode , and it's exactly what backprop does in chapter 4. Multiply right to left ( forward mode ) and you carry whole matrices along, which only pays off when there are few inputs and many outputs. Better still, nobody ever builds those m \times m matrices. The Jacobian of an elementwise \tanh is diagonal, so its vector-Jacobian product is just "multiply each entry by 1 - h^2"; for h = Wx it's "row times W". Every layer in a framework ships one small function: given the blame on my output, return the blame on my input.

sections.section: 1. Any smooth function is a polynomial, up close
sections.text: Calculus 1 replaced a curve by its tangent line near a point c. Why stop at a line? Match the value, the slope, the curvature, and so on, one derivative per term:  f(x) \approx f(c) + f'(c)(x - c) + \frac{f''(c)}{2!}(x - c)^2 + \frac{f'''(c)}{3!}(x - c)^3 + \dots  f(x) = eˣ sin x ln(1 + x) center c order f its Taylor polynomial Order 0 is a flat line, order 1 the tangent, order 2 a parabola that also bends the right way. Each new term hugs the curve over a wider stretch. For e^x and \sin x adding terms eventually works everywhere; for \ln(1+x) around 0 it only helps for x between −1 and 1, and beyond that more terms make it worse . Try it. Near any point, a smooth function is its value, plus slope times the step, plus half the curvature times the step squared, plus terms that shrink fast. ML lives on the first two. ML lives almost entirely on the first two orders. The loss near the current weights is a slope plus a curvature: L(w + \Delta) \approx L(w) + L'(w)\,\Delta + \tfrac12 L''(w)\,\Delta^2. The next sections are this one line put to work.

sections.section: 2. Why gradient descent works, and when it blows up
sections.text: Gradient descent steps \Delta = -\eta L'. Put that into the second-order picture:  L(w - \eta L') \approx L - \eta L'^2 + \tfrac12 L'' \eta^2 L'^2 = L - \eta L'^2 \left(1 - \tfrac12 \eta L''\right)  For small \eta the loss drops: that's the guarantee. But the bracket turns negative once \eta > 2/L'': the step overshoots so far that the far side of the valley is higher than where you started. The cleanest case is the parabola L = \tfrac12 k w^2, with slope kw and curvature k everywhere. One step does w \leftarrow w - \eta k w = (1 - \eta k)\,w. Each step multiplies the distance to the bottom by 1 - \eta k: curvature k learning rate η steps Below \eta = 1/k the ball creeps down one side. At exactly 1/k it lands on the bottom in one step. Between 1/k and 2/k it overshoots and bounces, but each bounce is smaller. Past 2/k every bounce is bigger: the loss goes to infinity, the "loss is NaN" you'll see in real training. A real network has different curvatures in different directions, and the steepest one sets the limit for all of them. A step is safe as long as the curvature can't turn downhill into uphill before it lands: the learning rate must stay under 2 divided by the curvature.

sections.section: 3. Stretched valleys: the Hessian and the condition number
sections.text: With many weights, the curvature becomes a matrix of second partials, the Hessian H_{ij} = \partial^2 L / \partial w_i \partial w_j (it's the Jacobian of the gradient, from Calculus 2). Take the simplest valley, L = \tfrac12(b x^2 + a y^2): the Hessian is \begin{pmatrix} b & 0 \\ 0 & a \end{pmatrix}, gentle along the valley (b = 1, in x) and steep across it (a, in y). The ratio \kappa = a/b, the largest curvature over the smallest, is the condition number . steepness a η Newton's step gradient descent Newton Section 2's rule now applies per direction: η must stay under 2/a for the steep direction, so the gentle direction shrinks by only 1 - \eta b per step, under 1 - 2/\kappa. The steps needed grow in proportion to \kappa. Gradient descent zigzags across the valley while barely moving along it. Real networks have condition numbers in the thousands and up, which is why plain gradient descent is slow and why optimizers like momentum and Adam exist (stage 4). With many weights there are many curvatures. One learning rate must suit the steepest, so the gentlest crawls, and the condition number counts how much slower. Newton's method fixes it outright: step by -H^{-1}\nabla L instead of -\eta \nabla L. Dividing by the curvature makes every direction equally easy; on a quadratic it lands on the minimum in one step, whatever \kappa is. Tick the box. Away from a toy, Newton's method shows its real strength: near a minimum, the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. Here it is against gradient descent on f(x) = e^x - 2x, whose minimum is at x = \ln 2 (where f' = e^x - 2

Where the gradient is zero, the Hessian's eigenvalues (the curvatures along its principal directions, chapter 1's "stretch factors") decide what you're standing on: eigenvalues point picture all positive minimum a bowl: up in every direction all negative maximum a hilltop mixed signs saddle a mountain pass: up along the ridge, down across it In a million dimensions, a minimum needs a million curvatures to all come out positive. If signs were coin flips, that's 2^{-1{,}000{,}000}. So almost every flat spot a big network meets is a saddle , not a bad local minimum, and gradient noise is usually enough to slide off it. Random symmetric matrices show the trend:

The last layer of a network gives one raw score per answer, called a logit : any number, positive or negative. To turn scores into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1, we use softmax : raise e to each score, then divide by the total. p(i) = e score(i) / T / Σ e score(j) / T temperature T 1.00 Drag the scores. Only the differences between them matter: add the same amount to all three and nothing changes. A score 2 higher means about 7 times more likely (e² ≈ 7.4). The temperature divides every score first: low temperature exaggerates the differences until the top answer takes everything; high temperature flattens them toward a coin flip. Softmax turns scores into probabilities in which only differences count: each extra point of score multiplies the odds by e, and temperature stretches or flattens the differences.

To train, we need a number for "how wrong was that belief?". The standard answer: look only at the probability the model gave to the right answer, p , and take −log p . That's the cross-entropy loss , also called surprise: 100% sure and right means zero surprise; 1% on the truth means a lot. probability on the right answer 0.60 The curve shoots up near zero. That's on purpose: a model that's confidently wrong gets a huge loss, so its gradient is big and it changes a lot, while a model that's unsure gets a gentle push. It's the same log loss our single neuron used in chapter 3, now for any number of answers. Cross-entropy charges -\ln of the probability given to the truth: nothing for confident and right, no upper limit for confident and wrong.

A language model is this exact machine with one answer per word in its vocabulary. Given "The cat sat on the", it gives every word a probability. Then it has to pick one. Always picking the top word is called greedy; it's predictable and tends to repeat itself. Instead, models usually sample : roll a weighted die. Try it, and try the temperature.
