Once you have a picture of "normal", the odd ones are the points it explains badly: far from their neighbors (the distance to the k-th nearest neighbor), unlikely under a mixture (a low GMM density), or easy to isolate . That last one is an isolation forest : random trees that cut the data at random places, where an unusual point ends up alone after only a few cuts while normal points sit in crowds. Four error rates tell you where the trouble is. Human-level error stands in for the best possible (some inputs are truly ambiguous, so nothing gets 0%). Training error is on the data the model learned from. Train-dev error is on held-out examples from the same source as training. Dev error is on examples like the ones the model will meet in use. Slicing an array doesn't copy it. first_rows = X[:2] is a view : a new name looking at the same memory. Change the view and the original changes. That makes slicing instant even on a huge array, and it's a classic bug. Indexing with a list or a mask ( fancy indexing ) makes a copy instead, because the chosen items aren't evenly spaced in memory any more. A slice is a window onto the same memory; a list or a mask makes a copy; and an in-place change through a window changes the original.

Matrix products, dot products, traces, batch products: they're all "multiply matching entries and add some indices up". np.einsum writes exactly that. Each number takes a fixed number of bytes set by its dtype : 8 for float64 (NumPy's default), 4 for float32 (what deep learning uses), 2 for float16 . So an array's memory is just its size times that. Estimate before you allocate: it's the cheapest bug catch there is. Memory is size times bytes per number: estimate it before you allocate, and remember float32 keeps only about seven digits.

Chapter 11's L2 penalty adds \lambda w to every gradient, pulling weights toward zero. With SGD that's the same as shrinking every weight by a fixed fraction each step, called weight decay . With Adam it isn't: the \lambda w term goes through the division by \sqrt{s}, so weights with big gradients barely get pulled, and the penalty does something nobody intended. The best learning rate changes during training. Early on, the weights are random and Adam's averages are based on a handful of steps: a big step can throw the model somewhere it never recovers from. Late in training, the model is near a good spot and big steps bounce around it. So the rate is scheduled : a short linear warmup from near zero, then a slow decay . Training starts with a short warmup so early, unreliable steps stay small, then decays so late steps settle instead of bouncing.

During training, dropout sets each neuron's output to 0 with probability p (often 0.1 to 0.5) and scales the survivors by 1/(1 - p) so the expected total stays the same. No neuron can rely on one particular partner being there, so the network learns redundant, spread-out features, which overfit less (chapter 11). In use ( model.eval() ), nothing is dropped: it's like averaging the predictions of all the thinned networks seen in training. Dropout switches random neurons off while training, so none can lean on a particular partner, and scales the rest so the totals match use time.

A residual block outputs its input plus a correction: y = x + f(x). Chapter 7's transformer blocks are built this way, and so is ResNet, which first trained networks over 100 layers deep in 2015. Two things happen. The signal always has a path that skips the layer, so it can't vanish. And in backprop, the derivative of x + f(x) is 1 + f'(x): the blame reaching the top flows back to the bottom unchanged, plus whatever the layers add. A CPU has a few dozen fast, clever cores; a GPU has thousands of simple ones that all do the same thing to different numbers at once. A matrix product is exactly that: every output entry is its own dot product, independent of the others. So the work that dominates deep learning (chapter 1's matrix products, in every layer, for every example in the batch) is the work GPUs are built for. deep learning (chapter 1's matrix products, in every layer, for every example in the batch) is the work GPUs are built for. A FLOP is one multiply or one add, so an n \times n product costs 2n^3 FLOPs. Your browser's number above is probably between 1 and 50 GFLOP/s (it runs NumPy compiled for the web, on one core). That gap of four to five orders of magnitude is why nobody trains on a laptop CPU. A GPU is thousands of simple cores doing the same arithmetic on different numbers, which is exactly the shape of a matrix product.

A GPU can only compute on numbers it has fetched from its memory, and fetching is far slower than computing. An NVIDIA A100 does about 312 trillion bfloat16 FLOPs a second but moves only about 2 trillion bytes a second: it needs some 150 FLOPs per byte fetched to keep its cores busy. Big matrix products reuse each number thousands of times and get there. Element-wise work (adding, ReLU, normalizing) does one FLOP per number and spends its time waiting for memory. A GPU computes far faster than it fetches, so work that reuses each number many times (matrix products) runs at full speed and element-wise work waits on memory.

A GPU runs at full speed only with enough work at once, so throughput (examples per second) rises with batch size until the GPU is saturated, then flattens; memory grows the whole way. When the batch you want doesn't fit, gradient accumulation runs several small batches, adds up their gradients (PyTorch's .backward() adds, remember), and steps once: Same gradients as the big batch (exactly, for losses that are means and models without batch norm), a quarter of the activation memory, a bit slower. To repeat a run exactly, every random choice must start from a known seed: Python's, NumPy's, PyTorch's, and the data loader's shuffling. Seeding is for repeating a run (debugging, checking that a change really did nothing), not for judging one. A result that only holds for seed 42 isn't a result. Seed every source of randomness to repeat a run exactly, and vary the seed on purpose to measure how much results wobble.

A run is defined by its settings: data version, model size, learning rate, schedule, epochs, seed. Put them in one dictionary (or a YAML file), pass it to the training code, and save it next to the results. Then "what did run 17 use?" has an answer, and a new run is a changed config rather than an edited script. A config holds every setting of a run in one place, so a run can be described, repeated and changed without touching the code.

Record each run as one row: its config, its metrics, when it ran, the code version ( git rev-parse HEAD ) and the data version. A JSON-lines file (one JSON object per line) is enough to start; MLflow, Weights & Biases and TensorBoard do the same with charts and a web page. The point is the habit: every run gets logged, including the failures, so you can see what you tried. Log every run, with its config, code version, data version and metrics, so results can be traced and searches judged honestly.

YOLO ("you only look once") cuts the image into an S \times S grid. The cell that contains an object's center is responsible for it, and predicts its box. The network's output is a tensor of shape S \times S \times (\text{numbers per cell}): one prediction per cell, all computed in one pass, which is why it's fast. Tap an object below. grid 7 × 7 New scene A detector's output is a grid of predictions, and the cell holding an object's center is the one responsible for finding it.

Predicting a box's width from scratch is hard: a pedestrian is tall and thin, a bus long and low. So each cell gets a few anchor boxes , typical shapes taken from the training data (clustered with k-means, in fact). An object is assigned to the anchor whose shape fits it best (highest IoU when both are centered together), and the network predicts only a correction to that anchor: c_x = (g_x + \sigma(t_x)) \cdot \text{cell}, \quad c_y = (g_y + \sigma(t_y)) \cdot \text{cell}, \quad w = a_w\, e^{t_w}, \quad h = a_h\, e^{t_h} Here (g_x, g_y) is the cell,

it best (highest IoU when both are centered together), and the network predicts only a correction to that anchor: c_x = (g_x + \sigma(t_x)) \cdot \text{cell}, \quad c_y = (g_y + \sigma(t_y)) \cdot \text{cell}, \quad w = a_w\, e^{t_w}, \quad h = a_h\, e^{t_h} Here (g_x, g_y) is the cell, \sigma keeps the center inside it (chapter 3's sigmoid), and the size is the anchor's a_w, a_h stretched by e^{t}. An RNN is one small layer applied at every step. It takes the new input x_t and its own previous state h_{t-1}, and makes the next state: h_t = \tanh(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b), \qquad \hat y_t = V h_t The same W, U, b are used at every step, like chapter 6's filter is used at every position: one set of weights, any length of sequence. A request costs \text{cost} = n_{\text{in}} \cdot p_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}} \cdot p_{\text{out}} with prices per million tokens, output usually several times dearer than input. Latency has two parts: time to first token (reading the whole prompt) and then a steady rate of output tokens per second, the playground's readout. Loops. A model can keep calling tools forever, or call the same one again and again. Blip gets at most 4 rounds; after that it must answer with what it has. Prompt injection.
